endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Determine whether specific criteria are defined for how "significant" shifts in model performance within subgroups (if differing from overall population due to sample size/error), or in parity between subgroups, should be defined, with adequate justification for the choice of criteria.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Organizations should define quantitative subgroup performance disparity thresholds that trigger escalation or deployment pause when thresholds aren’t met.

endorsements.title: Machine learning for healthcare that matters: Reorienting from technical novelty to equitable impact
endorsements.quote: Develop and hold projects to explicit standards regarding fairness, equity, and maximally permissible performance disparities between demographic groups.

endorsements.title: The imperative of diversity and equity for the adoption of responsible AI in healthcare
endorsements.quote: Agreed thresholds for acceptable performance disparities should be established to protect underserved populations from AI-induced harm.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence and Corruption: Opportunities and Challenges in the Health Sector
endorsements.issuer: The International journal of health planning and management
endorsements.quote: Periodic audits of the models can ensure they are not disproportionately flagging one demographic or systematically overlooking certain elites.

endorsements.title: AI Triage in Primary Care: Building Safer and More Equitable Real-World Evidence
endorsements.quote: In practice, these can be operationalized by setting thresholds (eg, sensitivity gaps ≤5% between groups), with breaches triggering model review and corrective action.

endorsements.title: A Futures Framework for Clinical AI Governance: Anticipating Emerging Risks, Shifting Roles, and Regulatory Challenges
endorsements.quote: These thresholds should be defined prospectively according to the system’s intended clinical function, risk level, and potential consequences of error and may include minimum subgroup performance levels, calibration requirements, maximum allowable subgroup performance differences, and minimum sample-size or confidence requirements for reliable subgroup estimates.

endorsements.title: Achieving Equity in Generative Artificial Intelligence in Cardiovascular Medicine
endorsements.quote: Health systems should establish predefined performance thresholds across demographic subgroups prior to deployment to operationalize recalibration.

endorsements.title: A strategic pathway for the ethical development of AI tools in dementia care
endorsements.issuer: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
endorsements.quote: To maintain fairness (equitable performance across patient subgroups) and reliability (consistent performance over time), teams should define explicit, pre‐specified performance “re‐audit triggers,” established during development and calibrated to the tool's risk tier.

commentary.bottom_line: Nine sources, two CHAI governance documents and seven commentaries, advise health systems to set documented quantitative criteria for subgroup performance shifts and parity gaps, but no supplied study tests whether doing so changes decisions or patient outcomes. The recommendation currently rests on expert agreement rather than measured effect.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The support consists of two framework documents and seven commentaries. Consensus among these sources is consistent in direction, but under GRADE conventions expert opinion does not establish an effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

No supplied study measures how often subgroup disparities go unaddressed without prespecified criteria, or whether criteria lead to earlier review. One commentary offers a sensitivity gap of 5% or less between groups as an example trigger, but that figure is illustrative and has not been evaluated for missed harms or false alarms.

Several endorsing commentaries frame thresholds as protection for underserved populations. No supplied study examines whether prespecified thresholds detect disparities affecting Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, whose small sample sizes may produce wide estimation error.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments that use prespecified, sample-size-adjusted subgroup criteria with deployments that do not. Useful studies would measure consistency of escalation decisions across reviewers, time to detect a subgroup performance shift, false alarm rates in small subgroups, the burden of maintaining criteria, and downstream patient outcomes by subgroup.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. These groups are often small within a single health system's data, and it remains unknown whether criteria that account for estimation error would flag or miss disparities affecting them.
